Three results below are nulls. A null is nearly content-free without a resolution bound attached, so here is what each design could actually have detected.

Clustering moves within games costs a 2.18x sample penalty for the same resolution, and every bound above carries it.

Two published claims have been withdrawn

"Save rate falls monotonically with rating." An artifact of truncating evaluation at ply 120, which preferentially discarded long defensive games. Every game is now scored to its end.

"Amateurs save by winning, masters save by drawing." The contrast disappears once each group is normalised by its own base draw rate. Caught by falsification probe P1, which still fires.

Both retractions are pinned by tests, and the claims checker fails if the retraction text is removed while the probe still fires.

Findings

3Blunders, rating and thinking time

Blunder rate falls about 3.4x from 1200 to 2200. Faster games blunder roughly 29% more than slower ones, tested as a difference rather than by comparing interval overlap. Time control shifts the mean by a little; which two humans sat down shifts it by a lot.

5White's first-move advantage and draw rates

White scores above parity in every classical band and the edge grows with strength, a known result. Classical draw rates are rising, consistent with Ben-Moshe & Genesove (2026). An earlier build said the opposite; the tournament corpus had become majority online blitz from 2020, and that headline was retracted once a literature search exposed the contradiction.

2Do engine-approved openings win more?

No, at any rating. Nothing survives multiplicity correction and the sign of the rank correlation flips between bands. The mechanical reason is range compression: every mainline opening evaluates within a 26 centipawn band.

4Rating drift at a fixed rating

No detectable drift, replicating Regan & Haworth (2011) on overlapping data. Resolution is about +/-1.5 cp per decade, too coarse to settle either inflation or the deflation FIDE's own analysis documented.

8Rating drift, following the same players

Null again from a different design. Within one person, calendar time and career stage cannot be separated without an assumption: the standard age-period-cohort problem, reproduced here rather than discovered.

9Saving lost positions, format held constant

No gradient across 400 Elo of over-the-board play. Combined with the online sample, both corpora are internally flat and separated by a large step, which points at playing format rather than strength.

11Is the save-rate gap skill, or is it format?

The one result here that appears to be new. Lost positions are saved far more often online because over-the-board players resign. Comparing the same 558 titled players with themselves, 15.6% of their online losses end in checkmate against 4.0% of their classical over-the-board losses. Fast play at a board moves that only slightly; moving online moves it a lot. Checkmate is read from the move list, a method validated against board replay and Lichess's own tags with 100% agreement.

12An independent test, with players linked by FIDE ID

165,852 chess.com Titled Tuesday games, a source that shares nothing with TWIC except the players. Their checkmate share (18.1%) matches TWIC's online events (18.6%). Linking the same players by FIDE ID, their online losses end in checkmate 12.4 points more often than their classical ones, and 10.7 points more often than their over-the-board BLITZ losses, so the gap is not about speed. Online, about 30% of losses are time forfeits: playing on is partly a bet on the opponent's clock.

10Do the findings survive their own analytic choices?

Every defensible combination of analytic choices, then joint inference across the whole curve. The rating gradient survives (p = 0.002). The time-control effect agrees in sign in all 180 specifications but is only borderline jointly (p = 0.052), because every specification shares the same games.

7The track that attacks the others

Eight probes with pass conditions fixed in advance. One fires today and forced a retraction. Three others record bugs that were real. The largest error of all was caught by none of them: it was found by reading a paper whose result disagreed with this one.

Reproduce or reuse

pip install -e ".[dev]"
apt-get install stockfish
make data      # ~150 MB from GitHub mirrors
make build     # ~1h, engine-bound, resumable
make verify    # tests + claims check + manifest check

The engine evaluations are the only expensive artifact here, roughly an hour of single-core Stockfish. deadlost export writes them as 125,673 scored moves joined to game metadata, with a data dictionary documenting four traps, three of which produced real errors during this build.

deadlost limits prints every known confound and resolution bound. If you think a finding is wrong, there is an issue template for exactly that: it is the contribution this project most wants.
